hops.title: Why D-asparagine tastes sweet
hops.text: In 1886 the Italian chemist Arnaldo Piutti worked through 6,500 kilograms of vetch plants to collect 100 grams of D-asparagine, the mirror image of ordinary L-asparagine. Then he tasted it. Piutti found L-asparagine tasteless and D-asparagine intensely sweet. Same atoms, same bonds, opposite handedness, and the tongue noticed. Louis Pasteur remarked on how important the result was. It was the first reported case of a biological receptor responding differently to two mirror images, which means the taste sensors on your tongue, built from L-amino acids, must be handed too.

sources.citation: Gal J. The discovery of stereoselectivity at biological receptors: Arnaldo Piutti and the taste of the asparagine enantiomers--history and analysis on the 125th anniversary. Chirality. 2012;24(12):959-976.

hops.afterHeading: Four side-chain families, read from the switches
hops.title: Turkey and the tryptophan myth
hops.text: Every November, turkey takes the blame for the after-dinner nap because it contains tryptophan, which the brain turns into serotonin. Two facts undercut the story. Gram for gram, roasted turkey has about as much tryptophan as roasted chicken breast, and a good deal less than cheddar cheese. And tryptophan, with its bulky, nonpolar side chain, competes with other large neutral amino acids, including leucine, isoleucine and valine, for entry into the brain. In rats fed protein diets, blood tryptophan rose but brain tryptophan did not. Oddly, a carbohydrate meal did raise brain tryptophan in rats. Nobody has shown that the mashed potatoes and pie cause the nap either.

sources.citation: USDA FoodData Central, SR Legacy: roasted turkey, roasted chicken breast and cheddar cheese, tryptophan per 100 g (FDC IDs 171095, 171477, 173414).

hops.afterHeading: The payoff: one swap, two properties
hops.title: One amino acid swap behind earwax and body odor
hops.text: Whether your earwax is wet or dry usually comes down to one amino acid at position 180 of a membrane pump called ABCC11. That position lies in the pump's first predicted membrane-spanning helix. With tiny, uncharged glycine there, the pump works: earwax is sticky, and sweat glands release compounds that skin bacteria turn into underarm odor. Swap in bulky, positively charged arginine and cells break down much of the pump, probably because the new charge disrupts folding. The arginine version passes 95% in some East Asian populations, and people with two copies have dry earwax and less underarm odor, though not none.

audio.title: Sweet crystals, sprinting muscles and earwax
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories where one small feature of an amino acid turns up somewhere you would never expect: a nineteenth-century taste test, a racing greyhound, and your own ears.

First, mirror images. In eighteen eighty-six, an Italian chemist named Arnaldo Piutti worked through six thousand five hundred kilograms of vetch plants to collect one hundred grams of D asparagine, the mirror-image twin of ordinary L asparagine. Then Piutti tasted his new crystals. He found ordinary L asparagine tasteless and D asparagine intensely sweet. Same atoms, same bonds, opposite handedness, and the tongue could tell. Louis Pasteur and others remarked on how important that was. Here is why. If two mirror-image molecules give two different tastes, then the sensors on your tongue must be handed too, the way a left glove only fits a left hand. It was biology's first glimpse of handed receptors, and it came from a chemist willing to taste his own crystals.

Second, proton switches at work in muscle. You learned that a group buffers best when its p K a sits close to the working p H. Hard-working muscle puts that rule to the test. When a greyhound or a racehorse sprints, its muscles need energy so fast that they lean on pathways that work without oxygen, and hydrogen ions build up. Diving whales face long stretches of low oxygen too. A drop in p H can sap muscle power and add to fatigue. These animals all carry large amounts of small molecules built on histidine in their muscles, called histidine dipeptides. Across many species, the fast muscle fibers hold the most. The best known, carnosine, was discovered in meat in nineteen hundred. Others go by the names anserine and balenine. Carnosine sits in muscle at millimolar levels, and its p K a is six point eight three, right in the range that working muscle passes through as it turns acidic. Histidine's ring soaks up some of the extra protons, slowing the drop in p H.

Third, one side-chain swap that helps explain why earwax can be wet or dry. Cells in your ear canals and armpits make a membrane pump called A B C C eleven. Position one hundred eighty is in what researchers predict is the pump's first membrane-spanning helix. Most people of European and African descent have tiny, uncharged glycine there. That version folds properly and gets to work. It helps make earwax sticky, and it helps sweat glands release compounds that skin bacteria turn into underarm odor. Now swap that glycine for bulky, positively charged arginine. Cells tag much of the new version as damaged and break it down, probably because the added charge disrupts folding, so less of the pump is left to do its job. That arginine version passes ninety-five percent in some East Asian populations. People who inherit two copies have dry earwax and less underarm odor, though not none. One amino acid, one change in size and charge, and the result is sticky earwax or dry, flaky earwax.

So the next time you look at a table of twenty amino acids, remember these three stories. Handedness at the alpha carbon reached your tongue, and side-chain chemistry reached a sprinter's muscles and your ears.
